#!/bin/bash
#FLUX --job-name=train_qrecc
#FLUX --time=7-00:00:00
#FLUX --queue=amd-gpu-long
#FLUX --output=%n_%J.out
#FLUX --ntasks=1
#FLUX --cpus-per-task=10
#FLUX --gpus-per-task=1
# sbatch --mail-type="ALL" was omitted as Flux does not have a direct equivalent.
# sbatch --mem=100G was omitted. In Flux, memory requirements are typically managed by the queue or a more complex resource specification which is site-dependent.
# sbatch --gres=gpu:4g.40gb:1 was translated to --gpus-per-task=1. The specific GPU type '4g.40gb' is not a standard Flux option and is omitted. This may have performance implications if a different GPU type is allocated.

# making sure we load necessary module and activate right environment
# module restore

#module load ALICE/default # you can access the AMD software stack like this, also works for Intel nodes
conda init bash
source ~/.bashrc
# initialize conda 
# or:: eval "$(conda shell.bash hook)"
conda activate convgqr
echo $CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV
echo $PYTHONPATH
# # move local data to local scratch on the running node
# data_dir="/home/wangym/data1/dataset/qrecc"
# scratch_dir="/scratchdata/${FLUX_JOB_USER}/${FLUX_JOB_ID}"

# mkdir -p $scratch_dir
# echo "## Scratch_dir is: $scratch_dir"
# #cp -r $data_dir/* $scratch_dir

# test path and CUDA device
# # the pwd is the directory where the script is located
TEST_DIR=$(pwd)
echo "## Current dircectory $TEST_DIR"
echo "## Number of available CUDA devices: $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"
echo "## Checking status of CUDA device with nvidia-smi"
nvidia-smi

# # run script!
echo "## Running training script on qrecc dataset!"
dataset_dir='/home/wangym/data1/dataset/'
model_dir='/home/wangym/data1/model/'
train_dataset='qrecc'
train_file_path="${dataset_dir}${train_dataset}/new_preprocessed/train_with_doc.json"
log_dir_path="${model_dir}convgqr/train_${train_dataset}"
model_output_path="${model_dir}convgqr/train_${train_dataset}"
decode_type='oracle'

# to train with checkpoint, specify --train_from_checkpoint 
/data1/wangym/conda/envs/convgqr/bin/python train_GQR.py \
      --train_from_checkpoint \
      --pretrained_query_encoder="${model_dir}pretrained/t5-base" \
      --pretrained_passage_encoder="${model_dir}pretrained/ance-msmarco-passage" \
      --train_dataset=$train_dataset \
      --train_file_path=$train_file_path \
      --log_dir_path=$log_dir_path \
      --model_output_path=$model_output_path \
      --collate_fn_type="flat_concat_for_train" \
      --decode_type=$decode_type \
      --per_gpu_train_batch_size=8 \
      --num_train_epochs=15 \
      --max_query_length=32 \
      --max_doc_length=384 \
      --max_response_length=32 \
      --max_concat_length=512 \
      --alpha=0.5

echo "## Training Done!"
# # store data back to local , only copying files that have changed
#rsync -av --update $scratch_dir/* $data_dir

reasons: The format specifiers used in the `#FLUX --output=%n_%J.out` directive are incorrect. `%n` and `%J` are SLURM-style specifiers. Flux uses a different syntax, such as `{jobid}`, `{name}`, and `{user}`. A valid replacement would be `--output={name}_{jobid}.out`.
issues: The job requests a queue named `amd-gpu-long` but later calls `nvidia-smi` to check the GPU status. If the allocated node has an AMD GPU, this command will fail. The correct utility for AMD GPUs is typically `rocm-smi`.

The script hardcodes the full path to the python interpreter: `/data1/wangym/conda/envs/convgqr/bin/python`. After the `conda activate convgqr` command successfully modifies the `PATH`, it is more portable and robust to simply call `python`.

The translation comments note that the original `--mem=100G` request was omitted. Depending on the default memory allocation of the `amd-gpu-long` queue, this could lead to the job being killed by the system if it exceeds the available memory.
